title: Mary at the hour of our death
word: Mary at the hour of our death
hookLine: every Hail Mary asks her prayer now and at the hour of our death
tomorrow: can thinking about death actually make you happier?

cards: Hospital rooms at night have their own sounds: a machine that beeps, a cart in the hallway, somebody's TV through the wall. Families sit there and run out of words.
When the words run out in a Catholic family, someone may start a Hail Mary. Nobody plans it. It's simply the words that are already there.
And the prayer already knows where it is. Its last line asks Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death. Why there?

teach.b: Because she's been there. John's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." She stood, and watched her son die.

Then, from the cross, Jesus gives her away, to the disciple he loved: "Behold thy mother." And John says from that hour the disciple took her to his own. Catholics read that as a gift to every disciple.
Now look at the prayer. Its first half is from Luke: the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's blessing. Its second half is the Church asking: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners.
Then just two moments: now, and the hour of our death. Every other moment of your life fits between them. That's the surprise.
A prayer people often say fast, for small things, has been rehearsing the biggest moment all along.
Said every day, it means that when the hour comes, the words are already there, and so, Catholics trust, is she. Notice whose prayer is asked for: not a formula's, a mother's.
Catholics ask Mary to pray with them, never to take God's place.

how: Catholics pray the Hail Mary daily, alone or in the rosary, and families often pray it at the bedside of someone who is dying.

games.q: what does “mary at the hour of our death” mean?
o: a promise that Catholics never die in pain
a blessing said only by a priest at a deathbed
asking Mary to pray for us when we die

games.q: what's inside the prayer — tap the pairs.
p: words from Luke: Gabriel and Elizabeth
Jesus gives Mary to the disciple

s: the whole Hail Mary comes word for word from the Bible
the first half is from Luke; the second half is the Church's own asking.
John says Mary stood by the cross
there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother.
the hour of our death line is only for people who are dying
it's prayed every time, so the words are ready when the hour comes.

games.q: your friend's grandmother is dying. the family asks you to lead a prayer, and you only know the Hail Mary, fast. what fits?
o: pray it slowly, one phrase at a time, with the family.
look up a longer, more impressive prayer on your phone.
say no; a rushed old prayer might come out wrong.
games.why: the Hail Mary already knows where it is: now and at the hour of our death. said slowly, it's a deathbed prayer.

practice: Sit with your hands open on your knees. Pray one Hail Mary as slowly as you can, a breath for each phrase, and let the last line land: now, and at the hour.
If that prayer isn't yours, sit with the face of someone you'd want beside you at the end.

wordCard.voice: Mary at the hour of our death. The mother who stood by the cross, asked to stand by ours.

orig.note: Latin: at the hour of our death. the last words of the Ave Maria before the Amen.

carryVoice: Your line: at the hour. She stood by the cross once, and Catholics trust she'll stand by ours. Go gently.

sources.q: there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother
